title.narrative: DRA Myanmar Earthquake ACJR 2025

description.narrative: On March 28, 2025, Myanmar was struck by powerful earthquakes of magnitudes 7.7 and 6.4, marking the strongest seismic events in the country since 1946. The affected region is home to 1.3 million internally displaced persons (IDPs), representing one-third of the total displaced population in Myanmar, further exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation. The impact of the earthquakes has been devastating across multiple regions. In Mandalay, Myanmar’s second largest city, media reports indicate that numerous buildings have crumbled, while in Naypyidaw, the capital, roads have buckled, further complicating relief operations. Power and communication outages have beenreported across affected areas, leaving millions without access to vital information. Roads, bridges, and other critical infrastructure have been severely damaged or completely destroyed, hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid. In response to the crisis, authorities have declared a state of emergency across six regions,affecting more than 28 million people, including an estimated 6.7 million children.The earthquake struck a nation already in turmoil due to over four years of civil conflict triggered by the military coup in 2021. The ongoing war between the junta and ethnic armed groups has severely weakened Myanmar’s healthcare system, making it ill-equipped to handle a disaster of this magnitude. In conflict zones such as Chin, Magway, Mandalay, and Sagaing, civilians are now at heightened risk, as fighting between military forces and resistance groups continues unabated. The situation demands urgent international assistance to address immediate humanitarian needs, including medical aid, shelter, and food supplies for millions affected by this catastrophe.

The sudden onset acute crisis joint response (JR) will be implemented in Mandalay and Sagaing regions, central Myanmar. To optimize aid coverage of the area, the DRA partners are responding in different townships in Mandalay and Sagaing, with a strong focus on Mandalay, closest to the earthquakes epicentre. Through theresponse, DRA covers needs in WASH, Health, Protection and MPCA. The partners have harmonized their approaches for MPCA, providing the standard MEB which covers one month basic needs.WASH35,080 individuals will be reached with critical WASH services, preventing waterborne diseases such as cholera and providing dignified sanitary services. This will involve the distribution of hygiene kits, including soap, distribution of dignity kits, providing emergency latrines to ensure safe sanitation facilities and prevent disease outbreaks, reaching a total of 35,080 people. Additionally, much needed access to clean water will be provided through pumping from water sources. Water storage tanks, drinking water containers and water purification tablets will also be distributed, ensure safe storage of water.Health2 Mobile Medical Teams (MMT) will be deployed, incl. 1 medical doctor, 2 nurses, 1 health counsellor and 1 health promotor, providing emergency primary healthcare and MHPSS services and referrals based on IRC/health sector guidelines. IRC procures medical supplies as well as uses pre-existing stock to ensure that the MMTs are equipped.ProtectionProtection needs have risen due to kids and women being exposed to higher risk. Protection needs are addressed through Psychosocial first aid through trained community volunteers in the mobile friendly spaces. Complex cases will be referred. Awareness sessions on protection, PSEA, and safe use of cash will be ensure safe, dignified, and informed access to assistance. GBV awareness and support is provided and protection monitoring will coordinate with health and cash team as well as other JR members for the referrals of the individuals identified with specific needs for healthcare or basic needs. Protection is mainstreamed throughout all other activities, such as staff being trained on PSEA.MPCAAs aid logistics are severely hampered due to the earthquake’s impact on vital infrastructure, MPCA is considered an essential modality until further aid is mobilized. All six partners in this JR will distribute cash in the first monthsof the response, allowing vulnerable people to flexibly meet their needs in WASH, Shelter, Food and Health. DRA partners harmonized their cash values (360.000 MMK/month), covering a month basic needs in line with the CMWG recommended transfer value. Markets in Mandalay are partly functional, despite some shops being closed or less accessible. This has already caused some prices to increase, but currently markets have been restored.

title.narrative: Joint Response webpage
WSH-R2 Excreta disposal

description.narrative: Access: ratio (user/facility) of 1 toilet for a max. 20 people, distance < 50 metres from dwellings, or as locally agreed. Clean: regular cleaning and maintenance for public facilities.Dignified: Use of toilets respect cultural preference and is arranged by household(s) and/or segregated by sex. Unsafe facilities: unstable (unlined) pits with risk of collapse, pits accessible to vectors, pits contaminating water tables and poorly sited facilities which expose women and girls to attacks, especially at night. Functional facility: fully constructed, in working order and properly maintained, of a type and in a location acceptable to intended users, with hand washing facilities and anal cleansing material.

title.narrative: WSH R-1 Hygiene promotion

description.narrative: Regular and timely access: 250g soap/p/m for personal hygiene, 200g soap/p/month for laundry. This includes hygiene/dignity kits. title.narrative: WSH-R4 Water supply

description.narrative: "Access: maximum distance to water point 500m, queuing time less than 15min, filling time maximum 3 min/20 litres or as locally agreed. Water access should be during the whole period of implementation unless action is mostly related to building the local water delivery capacity. Sufficient: covering basic needs, i.e. 7.5-15 l/p/d or as locally agreed. Safe: 1) low risk of faecal contamination, 2) No faecal coliforms detectable in any 100-ml sample, 3) For piped water supplies, or for all water supplies at times of risk or presence of diarrhoea epidemic, water is treated with a disinfectant to achieve free chlorine residual at the tap of 0.5 mg per litre and turbidity is below 5 NTU, 4) If for a short period, water which is contaminated chemically or radiologically is used, no (significant probability of) negative health effect is (likely to be) detected. Domestic use: drinking, cooking and personal hygiene (incl. laundry)"

title.narrative: PRO-R11 Gender-based violence (prevention, response, other)
Number of persons reached by the implementation of specific GBV prevention measures

description.narrative: 1) Preventive measure must be built on a thorough analysis of the risks and should - as much as possible - be designed to provide concrete changes in the short/medium term. Changes must be measured in the course of the action. Preventive measure should focus on the increased risks resulting from the crisis, rather than more structural issues. 2) Use the activity description field to to describe what measures are foreseen (sensitisation, infrastructure, etc.).3) Number of persons reached by prevention measures must be disaggregated by age and sex at reporting stage.4) If action also includes response activities, please add a custom indicator to reflect this.

title.narrative: PRO-R2 Prevention and response to violence
Number of persons who receive an appropriate response

description.narrative: 1) This indicator covers response to people (adults and children) having been victims of all kinds of violence. If the response provided is solely for suvivors of GBV, please select the GBV sub-sector.2) Appropriate response is defined as the provision of comprehensive services/assistance based on a thorough analysis of the risks faced by persons. The protection outcome of the response must be well defined. Relevant SOPs (including functional Referral Mechanism) should be followed.3) Use the activity description field to describe what services (medical, MHPSS, legal, security, etc.) are foreseen, as well as the SOPs in place.4) Number of persons must be disaggregated by age and sex at reporting stage.5) If action also includes prevention activities, please add a custom indicator to reflect this.Please note that response to GBV is captured under PRO-I12.

title.narrative: PRO-R12 Gender based violence (prevention, response, other)
Number of survivors who receive an appropriate response to GB

description.narrative: 1) This indicator covers response to survivors of GBV (women, men, girls and boys).2) Appropriate response is defined as the provision of comprehensive services/assistance based on a thorough analysis of the risks faced by persons. The protection outcome of the response must be well defined. Relevant SOPs (including functional Referral Mechanism) should be followed. 3) Use the activity description field to describe what services (medical, MHPSS, legal, security, etc.), as well as SOPs in place.4) Number of persons must be disaggregated by age and sex at reporting stage.5) If action also includes prevention activities, please add a custom indicator to reflect this.In case it concerns medical care to GBV survivors, please capture this under HEA-I8.

title.narrative: ACC-R2 Adaptations to JR
Number of adaptations in the design and/or implementation of the JR, as a result of the input from beneficiaries.

description.narrative: Active participation of beneficiaries could lead to concrete proposals in programme design and/or on how to improve existing implementation. In the activity description/comment field, indicate how this input from beneficiaries is gathered (planned) and at mid/end-term stage, what input was received from beneficiaries and to which adaptations this has led.

title.narrative: ACC-R1 Participation
Number of crisis-affected people who are also involved in the design, implementation, monitoring and/or evaluation of the programme

description.narrative: Participation is defined as the involvement of crisis-affected people in one or more phases of the programme: assessment, design, implementation, monitoring or evaluation. Participation does not take place when activities are carried out in exchange for a salary of 'in-kind' payment unless the affected people are involved in decision-making processes and have an impact on decisions that affect them.Please describe in the actvity description what this involvement specifically entails and in which phase of the program conflict-affected people are involved.

title.narrative: LOC-R3 Capacity Strengthening (reach)
Number of national and local actors supported with capacity strengthening

description.narrative: Please mention here the total number of national and local actors that received capacity-building support during implementation. In case more than one individual from a national/local actor participate in the capacity building activities, please only count this actor once. Note that this does not include local offices of INGOs.

title.narrative: LOC-R1 National and local actors
% of budget that went to national and local actors

description.narrative: This concerns Local Implementing Partner Costs. Please divide Local Implementing Partner Costs by the Grand Total Budget (incl ICR) to calculate this percentage. Note that this does not include local offices of INGOs.

title.narrative: LOC-R2 Capacity Strenghtening (localisation)
% of budget spent on capacity strengthening of national an local actors

description.narrative: This concerns capacity building such as training and on the job support to national and local actors. This is captured under "Capacity building local partners" in the DRA budget. Please divide Capacity building local partner costs by the Grand Total Budget (incl. ICR) to calculate this percentage. Note that this does not include local offices of INGOs.

title.narrative: CSH-R1 Unconditional and unrestricted cash
Number of people benefitting from unconditional and unrestricted cash transfers

description.narrative: Unconditional transfers are provided to beneficiaries without the recipient having to do anything in return in order to receive the assistance . Unrestricted transfers can be used entirely as the recipient chooses i.e. there are no restrictions on how the transfer is spent (Definitions of CALP). It can be delivered e.g. through local banks, shops, traders, local money transfer companies, remittance companies and post offices in either one or several instalments. Please include in the activity description the amount and frequency of cash transfers (i.e. how often). In case beneficiaries receive multiple transfers (e.g. each month), please only count the beneficiaries once.
